title: Catalog: Schinzel: m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n > N_m (fixed m ≥ 4)
connection: Schinzel: m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n > N_m (fixed m ≥ 4) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ (log p)³/m at primes (Pomerance–Weingartner heuristic). Obstruction: none local for large n. Status: open for every m ≥ 4; Pomerance–Weingartner: N_m ≥ exp(m^{1/3−ε}) (most primes near exp(m^{1/3−ε}) fail). Mechanism: Brun–Titchmarsh upper bound on Type I/II solvable primes when count (log p)³/m ≪ 1; Poisson heuristic predicts transition to 'always' at p ≈ exp(m^{1/2+o(1)}).
why: Gives a one-parameter family crossing the dividing line: m/p moves from 'mostly false' to 'always true' as p grows; ES is m = 4 at the 'always' end. Very direct calibration.
first_step: Compute for m = 8..40 the largest exceptional prime up to 10^9 and fit log N_m vs log m (prediction exponent 1/2); does m = 4's empirical margin match?
alt_first_steps: [signature-0049] Check the PW lower-bound construction for exceptions and whether its mechanism (covering by many small primes) can be run at m = 4.
refs: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)
repo_note: Schinzel m/n exceptional sets treated for all m; N_m growth left open.

title: Odd greedy algorithm as a cautionary every-n problem
connection: The odd greedy expansion (always choose the smallest odd denominator) is conjectured to terminate for every rational with odd denominator, but this is open even though Breusch/Stewart show odd representations exist. ES has the same split: existence vs a specific algorithm. Keep proofs about existence, not about a fixed procedure (consistent with B1's bounded-procedure barrier).
why: Prevents investing in 'prove algorithm X always succeeds' routes that are harder than existence.
first_step: Run the odd greedy algorithm symbolically on 4/n and determine the exact condition under which it terminates within three terms.

title: Erdős–Tetali thin bases: random sets A with r_{A,k}(n) ≍ log n for EVERY n — the polylog pointwise regime, solved probabilistically
connection: Erdős–Tetali (1990): for every k there is a basis of order k with Θ(log n) representations of every large n. Same regime as ES (F04: polylog count, F01: every n, F21: pointwise), proved by independence + concentration (Janson/Chernoff) of the random set.
why: The cleanest proof that polylog-many expected witnesses CAN give pointwise existence — when witnesses are independent enough. ES's question becomes: are ES witnesses 'Erdős–Tetali-independent' at each p, and in what quantitative sense?
first_step: Estimate the dependency structure of the ES level events at fixed p (pairwise correlations over (u,B,C)) and compare with the Erdős–Tetali concentration hypotheses (bounded pairwise dependence, expected count ≥ C log n with large C).
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0089] Write the 'ES random model': Poisson(c log² p) per p ⇒ P(fail) = p^{−c log p}; compute c from data and compare to Elsholtz–Tao.

title: Erdős–Turán conjecture (a basis has unbounded r(n)) vs. ES's Linnik-type large values
connection: Erdős–Turán: if r_{A+A}(n) ≥ 1 for all large n then r is unbounded. ES's R(p) is unbounded (Linnik-type large values; F37) consistent with this shape; ES's word set is a 'basis' of the primes in a trilinear sense.
why: A trilinear Erdős–Turán-type theorem would say: a set of words covering all primes must have unbounded multiplicity — the converse direction (multiplicity forced ⇒ coverage) is what ES needs; clarifies the logical relation.
first_step: Check whether Erdős–Fuchs (no representation function is c + small error on average) applies to Σ_{n≤N} R(n) to give a lower bound on its fluctuations.

title: Large sieve inequality applied to the exceptional set with the C-form classes as the sifting classes
connection: Classical large sieve: if a set S ⊂ [1, X] avoids ω(q) residue classes mod q for each q ≤ Q, then |S| ≤ (X + Q²)/L with L = Σ_{q ≤ Q} μ²(q) Π_{p|q} ω(p)/(p − ω(p)). For the C-form, S = exceptional set avoids, for each prime a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), the single class r_{C,a} mod a — ω(a) = #{C : 4C | a + 1} = τ((a+1)/4)-ish. So L ≈ Σ_{a ≤ Q} #{C: 4C | a+1}/a ≈ Σ_a τ((a+1)/4)/a ≈ (1/2) log²Q. Hence |exceptions ≤ X| ≪ (X + Q²)/log²Q — with Q = √X: ≪ X/log²X. A quick, elementary exceptional-set bound; weaker than Vaughan but *structurally* it shows the exceptional set has density 0 with a log² saving that mirrors the log²p count.
why: Elementary, and its proof shape (large sieve with ω(a) ~ τ(a+1)) might extend to a *weighted* large sieve giving more; and it exhibits ES's exceptional-set bounds as a special case of sieving by 'divisor-many' classes.
first_step: Verify the computation of L carefully (sum over prime a only, or all a via the full large sieve with multiplicative ω); compare with Vaughan's exp(−c(log N)^{2/3}); check whether larger Q (via Montgomery–Vaughan with Q up to X^{1/2}) or Type II's extra (c,d) classes improve the exponent.

title: Sum of two squares p = a² + b² and the Hecke-angle of p vs ES-hardness
connection: Primes p ≡ 1 (4) have a Gaussian angle θ_p (p = a² + b²). Hecke Grössencharacters equidistribute θ_p. If ES-hardness (e.g. large least certificate level, or λ(p) large) correlated with θ_p, ES would interact with ℤ[i]-arithmetic.
why: It is cheap and tests whether the Gaussian structure that p ≡ 1 (4) brings carries ES information. A null result rules out a class of approaches.
first_step: For p < 10⁸, correlate min certificate level / λ(p) / N₋(p) with θ_p and with a mod small numbers.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0127] Also test cos(4θ_p), cos(8θ_p) for the Hecke characters of Q(i) (Kubilius) — expect null.

title: Frobenius coin analogies

why: If a certificate construction is additive in one coordinate, conductor bounds could convert families into eventual coverage.
first_step: For each ES modulus 4C, derive the largest missing admissible divisor residue from small data and seek a semigroup-style conductor bound.
